resources.string:
Welcome to the first ever lesson in our app! 

You will be learning the basics of Hiragana! 「ひらがな」 

Hiragana is one of the three main writing systems in Japanese or Nihongo. The other two are Katakana and Kanji. 

Hiragana → basic sounds and grammar 
Katakana → foreign words 
Kanji → complex characters with meaning 

Learning how to read Hiragana will bring you one-third of the way to reading Japanese and that is no joke. 

Let's get started!

We will be focusing on the basic sounds of Hiragana. These are actually familiar if you know English! 
These are A, E, I, O, and U. The only difference is the arrangement. In Japanese, these go in this order: 

あ い う え お 
or 
A		I		U		E		O 

This is known as the A or あ row. This will be your best reference for the sequence of the Hiragana alphabet.

The \"Ka\" row (か、き、く、け、こ) is the second row of the Hiragana chart. It is formed by adding the \"k\" sound to the vowels. This is one of the most common rows you will encounter in many basic words like \"kami\" (paper) or \"koko\" (here).
The \"Sa\" row (さ、し、す、せ、そ) introduces the \"s\" sound. A key thing to remember is that \"si\" is written and pronounced as \"shi\" (し). It sounds like the \"she\" in \"sheep\".
The \"Ta\" row (た、ち、つ、て、と) introduces the \"t\" sound. This row has two unique pronunciations: \"ti\" becomes \"chi\" (ち) as in \"cheese\", and \"tu\" becomes \"tsu\" (つ) as in \"tsunami\".
The \"Na\" row (な、に、ぬ、ね、の) follows the standard pattern of adding \"n\" to the vowels. This row is used in many common particles like \"na\" and \"ni\", and words like \"neko\" (cat).
Welcome to Hiragana Part 2! \n\nIn this lesson, we will cover the remaining characters of the basic Hiragana chart. These include the Ha, Ma, Ra, Ya and Wa rows, along with the single sound \"n\".
The \"Ha\" row (は、ひ、ふ、へ、ほ) introduces the \"h\" sound. Note that \"hu\" is pronounced as \"fu\" (ふ), like blowing out a candle.
The \"Ma\" row (ま、み、む、め、も) is straightforward, combining the \"m\" sound with the five vowels.
The \"Ya\" row (ya, yu, yo) only has three characters. They are formed with the \"y\" sound.

For (ら、り、る、れ、ろ), your tongue should flick the roof of your mouth once, very quickly, just behind your front teeth. It’s not a full \“r\” sound, there’s no curling or tension. It’s more like a light tap and release.

Finally, we have the "Wa" row (わ、を) and the single consonant "n" (ん). 

"Wo" (を) is primarily used as a grammatical particle and is often pronounced just like "o". 

"n" (ん) is the only Hiragana character that doesn't end in a vowel. It can also be pronounced as the letter "m"\ sound in some words.

Okay, get this. You actually don't have to learn a bunch of brand new characters right now. We can just upgrade the ones you already know! 

See these two little dashes? We call them "tenten". Think of them as a harder first letter. When you add them, the sound gets harder and you get the next row. 

And then there's this little circle, the "maru". It looks exactly like a tiny bubble, right? It's a special little rule that only works on the H-row to give it a popping sound.

Here is the neat trick to remembering all of these. Think of the tenten marks as just a "harder" version of the first letter: 

- K becomes G 
- S becomes Z 
- T becomes D 
- H becomes B 

Now for that little maru bubble. Just remember that bubbles "pop" as in the letter "p"
Welcome to Katakana Part 1! \n\nKatakana is mainly used for foreign names, places, and loanwords. It looks more angular than Hiragana, but the sounds are exactly the same!
The \"A\" row (ア、イ、ウ、エ、オ) is the base of Katakana. Notice how sharp and straight the lines are compared to Hiragana.
The \"Ka\" row (カ、キ、ク、ケ、コ) sounds like \"ka, ki, ku, ke, ko\". \"Ka\" (カ) looks very similar to its Hiragana counterpart.
The \"Sa\" row (サ、シ、ス、セ、ソ) includes \"shi\" (シ). Be careful not to confuse it with \"tsu\" (ツ)!
The \"Ta\" row (タ、チ、ツ、テ、ト) includes \"chi\" (チ) and \"tsu\" (ツ).
The \"Na\" row (ナ、ニ、ヌ、ネ、ノ) uses simple strokes. \"Ni\" (ニ) looks like the number two in Kanji.
The \"Ha\" row (ハ、ヒ、フ、ヘ、ホ) includes \"fu\" (フ).
The \"Ma\" row (マ、ミ、ム、メ、モ) follows the standard \"m\" sound.
The \"Ya\" row (ヤ、ユ、ヨ) only has three characters.
The \"Ra\" row (ラ、リ、ル、レ、ロ) sounds like a light flap, just like in Hiragana.
The \"Wa\" row (ワ、ヲ) and \"n\" (ン). \"N\" is frequently used at the end of foreign names.

Good news! The upgrade system you learned for Hiragana works exactly the same way here! \n\nJust like before, adding two small strokes (tenten) or a tiny bubble (maru) changes the sound. Since Katakana is mostly for foreign loanwords, these voiced sounds are everywhere from food brands to tech terms!

Let's refresh your memory with these tricks: 

- K becomes G 
- S becomes Z 
- T becomes D 
- H becomes B 
- H becomes P 

Remember that the same rule applies here like in the Hiragana lesson. That little maru bubble. Just remember that bubbles "pop" as in the letter "p"
Beyond the basic Hiragana and Katakana charts, Japanese uses several special characters and punctuation marks that are essential for reading and writing correctly.
The character ヴ is used in Katakana to represent the \"V\" sound, which doesn\'t exist in native Japanese. It is often combined with small vowels: ヴァ (va), ヴィ (vi), ヴ (vu), ヴェ (ve), ヴォ (vo).
The small ぅ (u) is less common than other small vowels but can be used in certain loanwords or to extend the sound of a preceding character in a stylized way, often in manga or informal speech.

The horizontal bar ― or ー (Chōonpu) is used to indicate a long vowel sound. In Katakana, it is extremely common (e.g., ケーキ - kēki/cake). In Hiragana, long vowels are usually written with extra vowels, but the bar is sometimes seen in informal writing or signs.
The wave dash ～ (Nami dasshu) is used to indicate a range (like \"from... to...\") or to show that a sound is being drawn out in a friendly or sing-song tone at the end of a sentence.
The exclamation mark ！ and question mark ？ are used just like in English, though traditional Japanese often uses the particle 「か」 at the end of a sentence instead of a question mark.

Japanese quotation marks are 「 」 (Kagi kakko). While English-style double quotes \" \" are also used (especially in digital media), the Japanese brackets are much more common in books and formal writing.

Kanji are logographic Chinese characters used in Japanese. Each character represents a meaning or concept. Learning them is essential for reading real Japanese text. Most Kanji have multiple readings: Onyomi and Kunyomi.
Japanese pronunciation is actually very simple because every character always makes the same sound. There are no silent letters like in English!
A (ah), I (ee), U (oo), E (eh), O (oh). Master these, and you\'ve mastered Japanese sounds.
Japanese is a rhythm-based language. Every character (mora) takes the exact same amount of time to say.
Most consonants sound like English, except for the \'R\' sound which is a light tap behind the teeth.
Some words change meaning depending on whether your voice goes high or low, like \'Hashi\' (bridge) vs \'Hashi\' (chopsticks).
Holding a vowel for two beats instead of one can change the word entirely! (e.g., Ojisan/Uncle vs Ojiisan/Grandfather).
The character \'n\' is unique because it can change sound slightly based on the next letter, sounding like \'n\', \'m\', or \'ng\'.

Reading Japanese is a rewarding journey that combines three different scripts. Once you know the characters, the next step is understanding how they flow together to form words and sentences. This lesson will guide you through the fundamental rules of Japanese reading.

In modern Japanese, text is often written horizontally from left to right, just like English. however, you will also see traditional vertical writing (tategaki), which is read from top to bottom, starting from the rightmost column.
Here are some common words written in Hiragana and Katakana. Try reading them aloud!
The small \"っ\" (tsu) or \"ッ\" indicates a double consonant. It acts as a brief pause in the breath before the next sound.
Vowels can be extended to change a word\'s meaning. In Hiragana, we add another vowel. In Katakana, we use a long dash \"ー\".
Small versions of ya, yu, and yo (ゃ, ゅ, ょ) combine with certain characters to create a single syllable.
Particles are small markers that show the relationship between words in a sentence. Note that some change their pronunciation when used as particles.
Though written as \"ha\", it is pronounced \"wa\" when marking the topic. Example: ねこ は かわいい (Neko wa kawaii) - Cats are cute.
Though written as \"he\", it is pronounced \"e\" when indicating direction. Example: とうきょう へ いく (Toukyou e iku) - Go to Tokyo.
This character is exclusively used as a particle to mark the direct object of a verb. Example: みず を のむ (Mizu o nomu) - Drink water.
